newsitem.title: RUSSIA: NASA astronaut to step in for ailing Mir commander.
newsitem.headline: NASA astronaut to step in for ailing Mir commander.

text.p: American astronaut Michael Foale is preparing to step in for the ailing Russian commander of the Mir space station in a risky repair operation tentatively rescheduled for next week, space officials said on Wednesday.
"We already understand that the commander cannot do this work because of his medical condition," Mikhail Sinelshchikov, head of the Russian Space Agency's manned flight division, told Reuters.

"There are two options, either it is done by the board engineer and Foale -- that decision will be taken after the results of the first test run, medical tests and a decision by NASA -- or put off to the next crew."
A three-man Russian-French crew is due to dock with Mir on August 7.

Mission flight director Vladimir Solovyov said a test run of the repairs had been set for July 21 after which a final decision on who would do the actual job -- tentatively rescheduled for July 24 -- and when would be taken in conjunction with the U.S. space agency NASA.
Sinelshchikov said the head of NASA had agreed with the head of the Russian Space Agency that Foale would get ready to replace Mir commander Vasily Tsibliyev for the complex repair undertaking.
"They agreed to carry on parallel preparations," Sinelshchikov said.
The current crew had been expected to undertake repairs later this week following a crash on June 25 between Mir and its unmanned cargo vessel, the worst accident in the station's 11-year history.
But Mission Control doctor Igor Goncharov told Tsibliyev, 43, on Tuesday that he needed to take it easy and go on medication after the discovery of a slight irregularity in his heartbeat.
"The commander will not participate in the repair operation. During the operation he, as the third member of the crew, will be in the escape apparatus," Goncharov said on Wednesday.
"We spoke to him and he understands his task and he is relaxed in this regard. We changed his participation because there are medical problems to be solved."

Sinelshchikov said Tsibilyev's irregular heart beat, which showed up in tests on Sunday, was mainly due to tension since the collision, which cut Mir's power supply in half. "It's not an illness of the heart, but a reaction of the heart to all the pressure."

Tsibliyev was to have manned the air lock between the main station and the damaged Spektr module while engineer Alexander Lazutkin tried to reconnect wires to the three undamaged solar panels attached to Spektr, now running idle.
The fourth panel is unlikely to be repaired.
Foale had originally been expected to sit in the Soyuz escape module ready to evacuate Mir crew if anything went wrong.
During a morning meeting, senior Russian experts from the agency that designed Mir as well as rocket engineers and space agency officials planned the next steps in the repairs.
Cosmonauts will have to wear bulky spacesuits in a cramped area of the sealed-off module to perform the operation, which is vital for the future of the ageing space station.

The latest problems have raised doubts over the future of Mir, the world's only space station. It is not due to be replaced until a planned new international space station Alpha goes into orbit in 1999.
But the Russian officials were adamant Mir should not be abandoned. "All of our experts say it is not rational to stop Mir operations," Solovyov said.
